## 6. When one step-set is everything

Although ($\ast$) is false in general, it is true under a natural extra hypothesis. The mechanism is a quotient argument coupled with the iterated Cauchy–Davenport inequality.

**Lemma 6.1 (Cauchy–Davenport).** For nonempty $A,B \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$, $|A+B| \ge \min(p, |A|+|B|-1)$.

**Lemma 6.2 (Iterated representation form).** Let $I$ be a finite index set, $c_i \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times$ and $T_i \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ nonempty for $i \in I$. Then the set
$$A = \Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_{i\in I} c_i s_i : s_i \in T_i\Bigr\}$$
satisfies $|A| \ge \min\bigl(p,\ \sum_{i \in I}|T_i| + 1 - |I|\bigr)$.

*Proof sketch.* Induct on $|I|$. The empty case gives $A = \{0\}$ and the bound $\min(p,1) = 1$. For the inductive step, $A_{I \cup \{a\}} = c_a T_a + A_I$; multiplication by $c_a \ne 0$ is a bijection so $|c_aT_a| = |T_a|$, and Cauchy–Davenport gives $|A_{I\cup\{a\}}| \ge \min(p, |T_a| + |A_I| - 1)$, which combines with the inductive bound. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (The conjectured bound holds when one set is full).** Let $p$ be prime, $k \ge 2$, let $v$ be pairwise independent, let each $S_i \ni 0$, and suppose $S_{i_0} = \mathbb{F}_p$ for some index $i_0$. If
$$D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1),$$
then $\mathcal{R}(v,S) = \mathbb{F}_p^2$.

*Proof sketch.* Let $I = \{1,\dots,k\}\setminus\{i_0\}$, so $|I| = k-1$, and put $c_i = \det(v_i, v_{i_0})$, nonzero by pairwise independence. Because $S_{i_0}$ is full it contributes $0$ to $D(S)$, so $\sum_{i \in I}(p - |S_i|) = D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$, which rearranges to
$$\sum_{i \in I}|S_i| + 1 - |I| \;=\; (k-1)p - D(S) + 1 - (k-1) \;\ge\; p .$$
By Lemma 6.2 the set $A = \{\sum_{i \in I} c_i s_i : s_i \in S_i\}$ is all of $\mathbb{F}_p$. Now fix a target $t$. Choose $s_i \in S_i$ ($i \in I$) with $\sum_{i\in I} c_i s_i = \det(t, v_{i_0})$ and put $w = \sum_{i \in I} s_i v_i$. By bilinearity $\det(w, v_{i_0}) = \sum_{i\in I} c_i s_i = \det(t,v_{i_0})$, so $\det(t - w, v_{i_0}) = 0$ and hence $t - w = a\,v_{i_0}$ for some $a \in \mathbb{F}_p$ (using $v_{i_0} \ne 0$, which follows from pairwise independence and $k \ge 2$). Since $S_{i_0} = \mathbb{F}_p$, the coefficient $a$ is admissible, and $t = w + a v_{i_0} \in \mathcal{R}(v,S)$. $\square$

**Remark 6.4.** The computation in the proof shows the numerics are tight: $(k-2)(p-1)$ is *precisely* the largest deficiency for which the Cauchy–Davenport estimate over the $k-1$ non-distinguished directions still reaches $p$. This is a second, independent derivation of the conjectured threshold — and an explanation of why it looked inevitable.

---

## 7. What the conjectured bound really buys

Theorem 6.3 used the full set only in the last step, to slide along $v_{i_0}$. Dropping that hypothesis, the first part of the argument still delivers a genuine theorem for arbitrary configurations.

**Theorem 7.1 (Surjectivity onto every quotient line).** Let $p$ be prime, $k \ge 2$, let $v$ be pairwise independent and each $S_i \ni 0$, and suppose $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$. Then for every index $i_0$ and every $c \in \mathbb{F}_p$ there is $r \in \mathcal{R}(v,S)$ with $\det(r, v_{i_0}) = c$. Equivalently, the image of $\mathcal{R}(v,S)$ in the quotient $\mathbb{F}_p^2 / \langle v_{i_0}\rangle \cong \mathbb{F}_p$ is everything.

*Proof sketch.* As in Theorem 6.3, put $I = \{1,\dots,k\}\setminus\{i_0\}$ and $c_i = \det(v_i,v_{i_0}) \ne 0$. Since $\sum_{i \in I}(p-|S_i|) \le D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$, Lemma 6.2 gives $\{\sum_{i\in I}c_is_i : s_i \in S_i\} = \mathbb{F}_p$. Choose $s_i \in S_i$ ($i \in I$) realising $c$ and set $s_{i_0} = 0 \in S_{i_0}$. The point $r = \sum_i s_i v_i$ lies in the reach and, because $\det(v_{i_0},v_{i_0}) = 0$, satisfies $\det(r, v_{i_0}) = \sum_{i \in I} c_i s_i = c$. $\square$

**Corollary 7.2 (No missing line).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1, for every $i_0$ and every $b \in \mathbb{F}_p^2$ there is $t \in \mathbb{F}_p$ with $b + t\,v_{i_0} \in \mathcal{R}(v,S)$. That is, the complement of the reach contains no full line in any of the $k$ directions.

*Proof sketch.* Apply Theorem 7.1 with $c = \det(b, v_{i_0})$ to get $r \in \mathcal{R}(v,S)$ with $\det(r - b, v_{i_0}) = 0$; then $r - b$ is a multiple of $v_{i_0}$. $\square$

**Remark 7.3.** Corollary 7.2 confines any counterexample to a sparse missed set: at most $p-1$ points on each line in each of the $k$ directions could conceivably be missed, but no line entirely. The harmonic family sits at the extreme opposite end of this range, missing a single point out of $p^2$ — a failure that is real but minimal.

---

## 8. The polynomial-method reformulation

We now explain analytically why $(k-2)(p-1)$ is the "right-looking" bound, and locate exactly the step that fails.

**Definition 8.1 (Coordinate linear forms).** For a direction family $v = (v_1,\dots,v_k)$ define, in the polynomial ring $\mathbb{F}_p[X_1,\dots,X_k]$,
$$L_1 = \sum_{i=1}^k (v_i)_1 X_i, \qquad L_2 = \sum_{i=1}^k (v_i)_2 X_i .$$
For $x \in \mathbb{F}_p^k$ one has $\bigl(L_1(x), L_2(x)\bigr) = \sum_i x_i v_i$, so hitting the target $t$ means solving $L_1 = t_1$, $L_2 = t_2$ with $x_i \in S_i$.

**Theorem 8.2 (Nonvanishing-coefficient criterion).** Let $p$ be prime and let $e = (e_1,\dots,e_k)$ be exponents with
$$e_i < |S_i| \ \ \text{for all } i, \qquad \sum_i e_i = 2(p-1) .$$
If the coefficient of $\prod_i X_i^{e_i}$ in $L_1^{\,p-1}L_2^{\,p-1}$ is nonzero, then $\mathcal{R}(v,S) = \mathbb{F}_p^2$.

*Proof sketch.* Fix a target $t$ and set
$$F = \bigl(1 - (L_1 - t_1)^{p-1}\bigr)\bigl(1 - (L_2 - t_2)^{p-1}\bigr) .$$
Expanding $F = 1 - A - B + AB$ with $A = (L_1-t_1)^{p-1}$, $B = (L_2-t_2)^{p-1}$: the terms $1$, $A$, $B$ have total degree $< 2(p-1)$ and so contribute nothing to the coefficient at $e$; and $AB$ differs from $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ only in degrees $< 2(p-1)$, because replacing a linear form $f$ by $f - c$ changes $f^n$ only below degree $n$. Hence the coefficient of $X^e$ in $F$ equals that in $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$, which is nonzero by hypothesis; and $\deg F = 2(p-1) = \sum_i e_i$. The Combinatorial Nullstellensatz then supplies $x$ with $x_i \in S_i$ and $F(x) \ne 0$. Both factors of $F$ are then nonzero, and by Fermat's little theorem $1 - y^{p-1} \ne 0$ forces $y = 0$; thus $L_1(x) = t_1$ and $L_2(x) = t_2$, i.e. $\sum_i x_i v_i = t$. $\square$

**Definition 8.3 (Admissible exponent vector).** An exponent vector $e$ is *admissible* for $S$ if $e_i < |S_i|$ for all $i$ and $\sum_i e_i = 2(p-1)$.

**Theorem 8.4 (The degree budget equals the conjectured bound).** Let $p$ be prime, $k \ge 2$, and let each $S_i$ be nonempty. An admissible exponent vector exists **if and only if**
$$D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1).$$

*Proof sketch.* The maximum available total exponent is $\sum_i (|S_i| - 1)$, and
$$\sum_i (|S_i| - 1) = \sum_i \bigl((p-1) - d_i\bigr) = k(p-1) - D(S).$$
So a vector with $e_i \le |S_i|-1$ and $\sum_i e_i = 2(p-1)$ exists iff $k(p-1) - D(S) \ge 2(p-1)$, i.e. iff $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$; the "if" direction is realised by greedily filling the caps $|S_i|-1$ until the total $2(p-1)$ is reached. $\square$

**Theorem 8.5 (Structure of the conjecture).** Under $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$ with all $S_i$ nonempty, an admissible exponent vector $e$ always exists, and any admissible $e$ whose coefficient in $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ is nonzero proves $\mathcal{R}(v,S) = \mathbb{F}_p^2$. Consequently the conjecture ($\ast$) can fail **only** through the simultaneous vanishing of *all* admissible coefficients.

*Proof sketch.* Combine Theorems 8.4 and 8.2. $\square$

**Remark 8.6 (What happens in the counterexamples).** In the harmonic family the caps are $|S_i| - 1 = (p-2, p-2, 1, 1, 0, \dots, 0)$, summing to exactly $2(p-1)$: there is precisely *one* admissible exponent vector, namely $e = (p-2, p-2, 1, 1, 0,\dots,0)$, and its coefficient in $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ vanishes. The counterexample is thus not a violation of the polynomial method but a *witness that the method's hypothesis is strictly stronger than the degree count* — the conjecture ($\ast$) was the degree count mistaken for the hypothesis.

---

## 9. Algorithms

The results above are effective, and the following procedures make them so.

**Algorithm A (Reach computation by iterated sumset).** Given $p$, directions $v_1,\dots,v_k$ and step-sets $S_i$, compute $\mathcal{R}$ by starting from $\{(0,0)\}$ and repeatedly forming $\{r + s v_i : r \in \mathcal{R}_{\text{partial}}, s \in S_i\}$. Each stage costs $O(p^2 \cdot |S_i|)$ set operations and the accumulator never exceeds $p^2$ elements, so the total cost is $O\bigl(p^2 \sum_i |S_i|\bigr) = O(kp^3)$, versus $O\bigl(\prod_i |S_i|\bigr)$ for naive enumeration.

**Algorithm B (Spanning certificate).** Given a configuration, sort the deficiencies and test $d_{(1)} + d_{(2)} + d_{(3)} < p$. If it holds, output "spans" together with the explicit witness triple; by Theorem 4.1 this is a proof. Cost: $O(k\log k)$ after computing set sizes. This is the fastest available certificate and requires no computation in the plane at all.

**Algorithm C (Explicit representation along a triple).** Given a target $t$ and a certified triple $(i,j,l)$, compute $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ by Cramer's rule and scan $c \in \mathbb{F}_p$ until $c \in S_l$, $\alpha - \gamma c \in S_i$ and $\beta - \delta c \in S_j$. Theorem 3.1 guarantees success within $d_i + d_j + d_l + 1 \le p$ trials, so the cost is $O(p)$ field operations — an effective, worst-case-linear inversion of the three-line theorem.

**Algorithm D (Admissible-coefficient search).** Expand $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ as a sparse polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_p$ and inspect the coefficients at all admissible exponent vectors. A nonzero one is a spanning certificate valid even when no triple criterion applies. The expansion has at most $\binom{k + 2p - 3}{2p-2}$ monomials, so this is exponential in $p$ in general but entirely practical for the small parameters where the phenomenon lives.

---

## 10. Computational evidence

Exhaustive and targeted computations support and sharpen the theory.

* **Three-line theorem, exhaustively.** Over all pairwise independent triples of directions and all step-sets containing $0$: at $p=3$, all $88$ configurations with $D < p$ span; at $p=5$, all $15{,}880$ do. At $D = p$ exactly, non-spanning configurations appear ($80$ at $p=3$, $14{,}400$ at $p=5$), so $D < p$ is exactly the right hypothesis.
* **The counterexample family.** For $(p,k) \in \{(3,4),(5,4),(5,6),(7,5),(7,8),(11,6)\}$ the harmonic family is pairwise independent, has $D = (k-2)(p-1)$ exactly, and misses precisely the single point $(1,2)$.
* **Triple sharpness.** In the same family the minimum triple deficiency is exactly $p$ for every tested $(p,k)$, confirming Theorem 5.5 numerically.
* **Quotient-line surjectivity.** For the counterexamples the image of the reach in each of the $k$ quotient lines has size exactly $p$ — the reach meets every line in every direction, as Theorem 7.1 requires.
* **One full set.** At $p=5$, $k=4$, all $3{,}797$ configurations with $S_1 = \mathbb{F}_5$ and $D \le 8$ span, in accordance with Theorem 6.3.
* **Coefficient vanishing.** For the harmonic counterexamples the unique admissible exponent vector has coefficient $0$ in $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$; for a nearby spanning configuration at $p=5$, $k=4$ (with $D = 7 < 8$) there are three nonzero admissible coefficients.

---

## 11. Applications

**Covering and reachability with restricted alphabets.** A transmitter that can add rank-one contributions along $k$ fixed directions, each with a restricted alphabet, reaches every state of a two-dimensional register precisely when the reach is everything. Algorithm B gives an $O(k \log k)$ admissibility test, and Algorithm C an $O(p)$ decoder.

**Blocking configurations in finite planes.** The harmonic family produces, for every odd prime and every admissible $k$, a set of $p^2 - 1$ points that is a restricted sumset along $k$ directions and yet blocks a single point — an extremal object whose missed set contains no whole line in any of the given directions.

**Auxiliary-class exclusion arguments.** In classification problems where one wishes to exclude a *profile* of class sizes by showing that a corresponding spread must cover the plane, the conjecture ($\ast$) would have provided a uniform exclusion tool. Theorem 5.3 shows it cannot: in particular, the $p = 5$ profile $(8,2,2,2,2,2)$ cannot be excluded by ($\ast$), since the numerics of ($\ast$) are satisfied by non-spanning configurations. Theorem 4.1 gives the correct replacement tool, but with a genuinely stronger hypothesis.

**Design of step-set allocations.** Given a fixed deficiency budget, Theorems 4.1 and 5.5 say how to spend it: keep three of the deficiencies small, with sum below $p$. Concentrating the budget in the pattern $(1,1,p-2,p-2)$ on a harmonic quadruple is the uniquely wasteful allocation.

---

## 12. Discussion

The failure of ($\ast$) is a failure of *aggregation*. Total deficiency is a single scalar, while spanning is a projective-geometric property, and the harmonic quadruple is precisely a configuration in which a large budget is spent so as to create a genuine obstruction rather than diffuse slack. Two facts make this vivid.

First, the correct criterion is *local*: three directions with a joint deficiency budget below $p$ suffice, regardless of how impoverished the remaining $k-3$ directions are. Locality is the reason the criterion is robust; aggregation is the reason ($\ast$) is not.

Second, both natural derivations of $(k-2)(p-1)$ — the polynomial-method degree budget and the iterated Cauchy–Davenport count in a quotient line — are *correct as far as they go*. The degree count is exactly right (Theorem 8.4) and the quotient count is exactly right (Theorem 7.1); each simply proves a weaker conclusion than ($\ast$) claims. It is a good example of a conjecture that is not a wild guess but the conflation of a necessary condition with a sufficient one.

The overall picture is now complete in the following sense. For all $k$ and all $p$:

| Hypothesis | Conclusion | Status |
|---|---|---|
| $d_i + d_j + d_l < p$ for some triple | reach is $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ | true, and sharp |
| $D \le p-1$ | reach is $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ | true (special case of the above) |
| $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ and some $S_{i_0} = \mathbb{F}_p$ | reach is $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ | true, and the numerics are tight |
| $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ | reach meets every line in every direction $v_i$ | true |
| $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ | reach is $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ | **false** for all $k \ge 4$, $p \ge 3$ |

---

## 13. Future directions

**Profile dichotomy for spanning.** Fix $p$ and $k \ge 3$. Conjecturally, a deficiency profile $d_1 \le \cdots \le d_k$ (with $0 \le d_i \le p-1$) admits *some* pairwise independent non-spanning configuration if and only if $d_1 + d_2 + d_3 \ge p$ **and** the profile avoids an explicitly describable list of exceptions. The condition "the three smallest sum to at least $p$" is exactly the failure of Theorem 4.1, hence necessary; enumeration shows it is not sufficient. Every exception observed so far — $(0,2,3,3)$, $(1,2,2,2)$ and $(2,2,2,2)$ at $p=5$; $(1,3,3,4)$ at $p=7$ — is a profile in which no four indices can be arranged into a harmonic cross-ratio pattern with the available set sizes. The obstruction is projective, not merely numerical, and identifying it exactly is the central open problem.

**Cross-ratio invariants.** The harmonic quadruple is characterised by cross-ratio $-1$. Is a non-spanning configuration at the extremal deficiency necessarily supported on a quadruple in harmonic position, up to projective equivalence? If so, the exception list of the profile dichotomy would be computable from the geometry of $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)$ alone.

**Higher dimensions.** The three-line pencil argument generalises to $\mathbb{F}_p^n$ with $n+1$ directions in general position: is the correct criterion "some $(n+1)$-subset has deficiency sum $< p$"? The counting is suggestive, but the covering argument uses the one-dimensionality of the fibre in an essential way.

**Non-prime moduli and general abelian groups.** Cauchy–Davenport fails over $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ for composite $m$; the Kneser and Davenport–Erdős–Kneser theory replaces it with a stabiliser-corrected bound. The natural analogue of Theorem 4.1 would read: the reach is everything unless a coset of a proper subgroup obstructs. Formulating and proving the correct statement, with the subgroup correction, is open.

**Quantitative refinement of "no missing line".** Corollary 7.2 shows a counterexample cannot miss a whole line. The harmonic family misses exactly one point. Is *one* the maximum? That is: under $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$, is $|\mathbb{F}_p^2 \setminus \mathcal{R}(v,S)| \le 1$ always? Computation supports this for small $p$ and $k$, and a proof would show the conjecture ($\ast$) is false only in the mildest conceivable way.

**Effective inverse theory.** Given a non-spanning configuration, can one read off the missed point from the direction family and the set sizes in $O(k)$ time? For the harmonic family, the answer is $(1,2)$ up to the obvious projective normalisation; a general answer would turn the counterexample construction into a classification.

---

## 14. Summary of results

Let $p$ be prime, $v_1,\dots,v_k$ pairwise independent directions in $\mathbb{F}_p^2$, $S_i \ni 0$ step-sets, $d_i = p - |S_i|$ and $D = \sum_i d_i$.

1. **(Three-line theorem.)** For $k=3$: $d_1+d_2+d_3 < p$ implies $\mathcal{R} = \mathbb{F}_p^2$. Sharp.
2. **(Triple criterion.)** For any $k \ge 3$: if some three distinct indices have $d_i+d_j+d_l < p$ then $\mathcal{R} = \mathbb{F}_p^2$. In particular $D \le p-1$ suffices.
3. **(Refutation.)** For every prime $p \ge 3$ and every $k$ with $4 \le k \le p+1$ there is a configuration with $D = (k-2)(p-1)$ and $\mathcal{R} \ne \mathbb{F}_p^2$; the conjectured threshold is therefore invalid throughout the feasible range.
4. **(Optimality.)** In that same family every triple has $d_i+d_j+d_l \ge p$ with equality attained, so the criterion of (2) cannot be relaxed.
5. **(One full set.)** If some $S_{i_0} = \mathbb{F}_p$, then $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ does imply $\mathcal{R} = \mathbb{F}_p^2$.
6. **(Quotient surjectivity.)** $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ implies the reach meets every line parallel to every $v_i$; equivalently the missed set contains no line.
7. **(Polynomial method.)** $(k-2)(p-1)$ is exactly the degree budget making an admissible monomial of $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ available; a nonzero admissible coefficient certifies spanning, and the conjecture can fail only by simultaneous vanishing of all such coefficients — as it does in the harmonic family, where a unique admissible monomial has coefficient zero.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

Additive combinatorics over $\FF_p$ is dominated by one estimate: the Cauchy--Davenport inequality, $|A+B| \ge \min(p, |A|+|B|-1)$ for nonempty $A,B \subseteq \FF_p$. Iterating, a sum $A_1+\cdots+A_m$ of nonempty sets has size at least $\min\bigl(p, \sum_i|A_i|-m+1\bigr)$; in particular the sumset is everything as soon as $\sum_i|A_i| \ge p+m-1$, which is exactly the statement that the total deficiency obeys $\sum_i (p-|A_i|) \le (m-1)(p-1)$. The permitted deficiency grows by $p-1$ with each extra summand. The two-dimensional problem below is governed by an analogous-looking budget, and the point of this paper is that the analogy breaks.

The analogue replaces ``sets summed in $\FF_p$'' by ``sets of scalars applied along fixed directions in $\FF_p^2$''. Given directions $v_1,\dots,v_k \in \FF_p^2$ and step-sets $S_1,\dots,S_k \subseteq \FF_p$, the object of interest is
\[
  \Reach(v,S) \;=\; S_1v_1 + \cdots + S_kv_k \;=\; \Bigl\{\textstyle\sum_i s_iv_i : s_i \in S_i\Bigr\}.
\]
This is a \emph{restricted sumset along lines}: each summand is confined to a one-dimensional subspace, and the only freedom is how far along that subspace one may travel. Such configurations arise wherever a two-dimensional target must be hit by combining rank-one contributions with limited alphabets: covering codes, spread and blocking-set constructions in finite geometry, exclusion arguments for auxiliary-class profiles, and restricted-alphabet reachability analysis. The natural question is a threshold question: how depleted may the step-sets be before the reach fails to be everything?

\subsection{The conjectured threshold and the answer}

Two independent heuristics point to the same bound. First, a dimension count: two directions with unrestricted sets already span, and each further direction should buy a line's worth of slack, $p-1$, suggesting a budget of $(k-2)(p-1)$. Second, the polynomial method: Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz reduces spanning to the nonvanishing of a coefficient of $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ at an exponent vector $e$ with $e_i \le |S_i|-1$ and $\sum_i e_i = 2(p-1)$, and such an $e$ exists if and only if $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$.

So the conjecture
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conj}
  D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1) \;\Longrightarrow\; \Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2 \tag{$\ast$}
\end{equation}
is well motivated. Our results are: \eqref{eq:conj} holds sharply for $k=3$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:three}); it fails for all $k \ge 4$ and all $p \ge 3$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:counter}); the correct general criterion is a triple criterion (Theorem~\ref{thm:triple}) which is optimal (Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp}); \eqref{eq:conj} is valid when some $S_{i_0}=\FF_p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:full}); \eqref{eq:conj} always yields surjectivity onto every quotient line (Theorem~\ref{thm:quot}); and the degree-budget equivalence pins down the exact gap in the heuristic (Theorems~\ref{thm:cn}--\ref{thm:structure}).

\section{Definitions and conventions}

Throughout, $p$ is a prime and $\FF_p=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

\begin{definition}[Determinant]
For $a=(a_1,a_2)$, $b=(b_1,b_2)$ in $\FF_p^2$ set $\det(a,b)=a_1b_2-a_2b_1$. It is bilinear and alternating, and $\det(a,b)=0$ with $b \ne 0$ forces $a=\lambda b$ for a unique $\lambda \in \FF_p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Pairwise independence]
A family $v=(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ in $\FF_p^2$ is \emph{pairwise independent} if $\det(v_i,v_j) \ne 0$ whenever $i \ne j$; equivalently, the $v_i$ are nonzero and determine $k$ distinct points of $\PP^1(\FF_p)$. Since $|\PP^1(\FF_p)|=p+1$, necessarily $k \le p+1$; this is the \emph{feasible range}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Reach and deficiency]
$\Reach(v,S)=\bigl\{t \in \FF_p^2 : \exists\, s,\ s_i \in S_i,\ \sum_i s_iv_i=t\bigr\}$. The configuration \emph{spans} if $\Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2$. We write $d_i=p-|S_i|$ and $D(S)=\sum_{i=1}^k d_i$, and we always assume $0 \in S_i$ for every $i$.
\end{definition}

The hypothesis $0 \in S_i$ is a normalisation, not a restriction: translating each $S_i$ translates the reach by a fixed vector. Its combinatorial role is that a direction may always be \emph{ignored}, which is what makes sub-configurations usable: if $0 \in S_i$ for all $i$, then $\Reach(v|_I,S|_I) \subseteq \Reach(v,S)$ for every subset $I$ of indices.

\section{The three-line theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Three pairwise independent lines]\label{thm:three}
Let $p$ be prime, let $v_1,v_2,v_3 \in \FF_p^2$ be pairwise independent, and suppose $d_1+d_2+d_3<p$. Then $\Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Fix a target $t$ and suppose it unreachable. Since $\det(v_1,v_2) \ne 0$, the pair $(v_1,v_2)$ is a basis; write $t=\alpha v_1+\beta v_2$ and $v_3=\gamma v_1+\delta v_2$, where by Cramer's rule
\[
  \alpha=\frac{\det(t,v_2)}{\det(v_1,v_2)},\quad
  \beta=\frac{\det(v_1,t)}{\det(v_1,v_2)},\quad
  \gamma=\frac{\det(v_3,v_2)}{\det(v_1,v_2)},\quad
  \delta=\frac{\det(v_1,v_3)}{\det(v_1,v_2)} .
\]
Pairwise independence gives $\gamma \ne 0$ (else $v_3 \parallel v_2$) and $\delta \ne 0$ (else $v_3 \parallel v_1$).

Every representation of $t$ is determined by its third coefficient: if $s_3=c$ then necessarily $s_1=\alpha-\gamma c$ and $s_2=\beta-\delta c$, because $(v_1,v_2)$ is a basis. Unreachability therefore says that for every $c \in \FF_p$ at least one of $c \in S_3$, $\alpha-\gamma c \in S_1$, $\beta-\delta c \in S_2$ fails, i.e.
\[
  \FF_p \;=\; \Bigl\{\tfrac{\alpha-u}{\gamma} : u \notin S_1\Bigr\} \cup \Bigl\{\tfrac{\beta-u}{\delta} : u \notin S_2\Bigr\} \cup \bigl(\FF_p \setminus S_3\bigr).
\]
The maps $u \mapsto (\alpha-u)/\gamma$ and $u \mapsto (\beta-u)/\delta$ are affine bijections, so the three sets have sizes at most $d_1,d_2,d_3$, whence $p \le d_1+d_2+d_3$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The argument is a \emph{pencil} argument: the representations of a fixed target by three pairwise independent directions form a one-parameter affine family, and a missed target requires the parameter line to be covered by three forbidden images. Pairwise independence enters exactly twice, to keep the two coefficient maps non-degenerate.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Sharpness]\label{rem:sharp3}
For $k=3$ the conjectured bound $(k-2)(p-1)=p-1$ coincides with $D(S)<p$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:three} proves \eqref{eq:conj} for $k=3$, and it cannot be improved: $v=((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))$ with $S_1=S_2=\FF_p\setminus\{1\}$, $S_3=\{0,1\}$ has $D=1+1+(p-2)=p$ and misses $(1,2)$. Exhaustive enumeration at $p=5$ confirms spanning for all $15\,880$ hypothesis-satisfying configurations, and finds $14\,400$ non-spanning ones at $D=p$.
\end{remark}

\section{The triple criterion for many lines}

\begin{theorem}[Triple criterion]\label{thm:triple}
Let $p$ be prime, $k \ge 3$, let $v_1,\dots,v_k$ be pairwise independent, and let each $S_i$ contain $0$. If some three distinct indices $i,j,l$ satisfy $d_i+d_j+d_l<p$, then $\Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The subfamily $(v_i,v_j,v_l)$ is pairwise independent with total deficiency $<p$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:three} every $t$ equals $s_iv_i+s_jv_j+s_lv_l$ with admissible coefficients. Extend by $s_m=0$ for $m \notin\{i,j,l\}$, legitimate since $0 \in S_m$ and harmless to the sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:total}
If $k \ge 3$, the directions are pairwise independent, every $S_i$ contains $0$ and $D(S)<p$, then $\Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
Restated: the reach is everything as soon as the \emph{three smallest} deficiencies sum to less than $p$. Neither $k$ nor $D(S)$ enters; a single rich triple carries an arbitrarily deficient remainder.
\end{remark}

\section{Refutation of the $(k-2)(p-1)$ conjecture}

\subsection{The harmonic quadruple}

\begin{definition}
For $p \ge 3$ the \emph{harmonic quadruple} is $w_1=(1,0)$, $w_2=(0,1)$, $w_3=(1,1)$, $w_4=(-1,1)$. Its pairwise determinants are $1,1,1,-1,1,2$; all are nonzero precisely because $p$ is odd, and the slopes $\infty,0,1,-1$ form a harmonic range in $\PP^1(\FF_p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Blocking identity]\label{lem:block}
Let $s_3,s_4 \in \{0,1\}$ satisfy $s_1+s_3-s_4=1$ and $s_2+s_3+s_4=2$. Then $s_1=1$ or $s_2=1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Four cases. For $(s_3,s_4)=(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ the first equation gives $s_1=1$; for $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ the second gives $s_2=1$.
\end{proof}

The two equations are the coordinates of $\sum_i s_iw_i=(1,2)$. Thus with $S_1=S_2=\FF_p\setminus\{1\}$ and $S_3=S_4=\{0,1\}$ the point $(1,2)$ is unreachable, while $D(S)=1+1+(p-2)+(p-2)=2(p-1)=(4-2)(p-1)$.

\subsection{The uniform family}

Index directions by $0,\dots,k-1$ and set $v_1=(0,1)$, $v_3=(-1,1)$ and $v_i=(1,\lambda_i)$ otherwise, with $\lambda_0=0$, $\lambda_2=1$ and $\lambda_j=j-2$ for $j \ge 4$; the slopes are then pairwise distinct and avoid $-1$, which is possible exactly when $k \le p+1$. Set
\[
  S_i=\begin{cases}
    \FF_p\setminus\{1\}, & i \in \{0,1\},\\
    \{0,1\}, & i \in \{2,3\},\\
    \{0\}, & i \ge 4 .
  \end{cases}
\]

\begin{theorem}[Counterexample family]\label{thm:counter}
Let $p \ge 3$ be prime and $4 \le k \le p+1$. The configuration above is pairwise independent, every $S_i$ contains $0$,
\[
  D(S)=1+1+(p-2)+(p-2)+(k-4)(p-1)=(k-2)(p-1),
\]
and $(1,2) \notin \Reach(v,S)$. In particular \eqref{eq:conj} fails for every $k \ge 4$ and every odd prime.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Pairwise independence: $\det((1,\lambda),(1,\mu))=\mu-\lambda \ne 0$; $\det((1,\lambda),(0,1))=1$; $\det((1,\lambda),(-1,1))=1+\lambda \ne 0$ since $\lambda \ne -1$; $\det((0,1),(-1,1))=1$. The deficiency identity is elementary. For unreachability, in any representation of $(1,2)$ the padded coefficients are forced to $0$ and contribute nothing, so the coordinate equations reduce to Lemma~\ref{lem:block}, forcing $s_0=1$ or $s_1=1$ --- both forbidden.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exactly one missing point]
Computation over the harmonic family for $p \in \{3,5,7,11\}$ and all admissible $k$ shows the reach misses \emph{precisely} the single point $(1,2)$, consistent with (and sharpened by) the quotient-line surjectivity of Section~\ref{sec:quot}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Optimality of the triple criterion}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]\label{thm:sharp}
For every prime $p \ge 3$ and every $k$ with $4 \le k \le p+1$ there is a pairwise independent family of $k$ directions and step-sets containing $0$ such that (i) every triple of distinct indices satisfies $d_i+d_j+d_l \ge p$; (ii) some triple attains equality $d_i+d_j+d_l=p$; and (iii) $\Reach(v,S) \ne \FF_p^2$. Hence the strict inequality in Theorem~\ref{thm:triple} cannot be weakened to $\le p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Take the family of Theorem~\ref{thm:counter}, whose deficiency profile is $(1,1,p-2,p-2,p-1,\dots,p-1)$. A triple containing both indices $0$ and $1$ has sum $1+1+d_l \ge p$; any other triple contains at most one index of deficiency $1$ and hence at least two of deficiency $\ge p-2$, giving a sum $\ge p$ as well. The triple $(0,1,2)$ attains exactly $p$. Non-spanning is Theorem~\ref{thm:counter}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Combining Theorem~\ref{thm:counter} with Corollary~\ref{cor:total}, the largest valid $D$-threshold lies between $p-1$ and $(k-2)(p-1)-1$. But this is the wrong question: Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp} shows the honest invariant is not $D$ but $\min_{i<j<l}(d_i+d_j+d_l)$, for which the exact threshold $<p$ is now known.
\end{remark}

\section{When one step-set is everything}

\begin{lemma}[Iterated Cauchy--Davenport, representation form]\label{lem:icd}
Let $I$ be finite, $c_i \in \FF_p^\times$ and $T_i \subseteq \FF_p$ nonempty for $i \in I$. Then $A=\bigl\{\sum_{i \in I} c_is_i : s_i \in T_i\bigr\}$ satisfies $|A| \ge \min\bigl(p, \sum_{i \in I}|T_i|+1-|I|\bigr)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $|I|$; the empty case gives $A=\{0\}$. For the step, $A_{I \cup \{a\}} = c_aT_a + A_I$, and multiplication by $c_a \ne 0$ preserves cardinality, so Cauchy--Davenport gives $|A_{I \cup \{a\}}| \ge \min(p, |T_a|+|A_I|-1)$, which combines with the inductive bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The conjectured bound holds when one set is full]\label{thm:full}
Let $p$ be prime, $k \ge 2$, let $v$ be pairwise independent, each $S_i \ni 0$, and suppose $S_{i_0}=\FF_p$ for some $i_0$. If $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$ then $\Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $I$ be the complement of $\{i_0\}$, so $|I|=k-1$, and put $c_i=\det(v_i,v_{i_0}) \ne 0$. Since $S_{i_0}$ contributes nothing to $D(S)$,
\[
  \sum_{i \in I}|S_i|+1-|I| = (k-1)p - D(S) + 1 - (k-1) \ge p ,
\]
so by Lemma~\ref{lem:icd} the set $A=\{\sum_{i\in I}c_is_i\}$ is all of $\FF_p$. Given a target $t$, choose $s_i \in S_i$ ($i \in I$) with $\sum_{i \in I}c_is_i=\det(t,v_{i_0})$ and set $w=\sum_{i \in I}s_iv_i$. Bilinearity gives $\det(t-w,v_{i_0})=0$, hence $t-w=a v_{i_0}$ for some $a$, and $a$ is admissible because $S_{i_0}=\FF_p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The computation shows the numerics are tight: $(k-2)(p-1)$ is precisely the largest deficiency for which the Cauchy--Davenport estimate over the $k-1$ non-distinguished directions still reaches $p$. This is a second, independent derivation of the conjectured threshold --- and an explanation of why it looked inevitable.
\end{remark}

\section{What the conjectured bound really buys}\label{sec:quot}

\begin{theorem}[Surjectivity onto every quotient line]\label{thm:quot}
Let $p$ be prime, $k \ge 2$, $v$ pairwise independent, each $S_i \ni 0$, and $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$. Then for every index $i_0$ and every $c \in \FF_p$ there is $r \in \Reach(v,S)$ with $\det(r,v_{i_0})=c$; equivalently, the image of the reach in $\FF_p^2/\langle v_{i_0}\rangle \cong \FF_p$ is everything.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
As above, with $I$ the complement of $\{i_0\}$ and $c_i=\det(v_i,v_{i_0}) \ne 0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:icd} gives $\{\sum_{i \in I}c_is_i\}=\FF_p$. Realise $c$, set $s_{i_0}=0 \in S_{i_0}$, and note $\det(v_{i_0},v_{i_0})=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No missing line]\label{cor:noline}
Under the same hypotheses, for every $i_0$ and every $b \in \FF_p^2$ there is $t \in \FF_p$ with $b+t\,v_{i_0} \in \Reach(v,S)$: the complement of the reach contains no full line in any of the $k$ directions.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:quot} with $c=\det(b,v_{i_0})$ to get $r$ in the reach with $\det(r-b,v_{i_0})=0$; then $r-b$ is a multiple of $v_{i_0}$.
\end{proof}

Corollary~\ref{cor:noline} confines any counterexample to a sparse missed set. The harmonic family sits at the extreme end of this range, missing a single point out of $p^2$: a failure that is real, but minimal.

\section{The polynomial-method reformulation}

\begin{definition}
For a direction family $v$ put, in $\FF_p[X_1,\dots,X_k]$,
\[
  L_1=\sum_{i=1}^k (v_i)_1X_i, \qquad L_2=\sum_{i=1}^k (v_i)_2X_i ,
\]
so that $\bigl(L_1(x),L_2(x)\bigr)=\sum_i x_iv_i$. An exponent vector $e$ is \emph{admissible} for $S$ if $e_i<|S_i|$ for all $i$ and $\sum_i e_i=2(p-1)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonvanishing-coefficient criterion]\label{thm:cn}
If some admissible $e$ has nonzero coefficient in $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$, then $\Reach(v,S)=\FF_p^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Fix a target $t$ and set $F=\bigl(1-(L_1-t_1)^{p-1}\bigr)\bigl(1-(L_2-t_2)^{p-1}\bigr)$. Writing $A=(L_1-t_1)^{p-1}$, $B=(L_2-t_2)^{p-1}$ and expanding $F=1-A-B+AB$: the terms $1$, $A$, $B$ have total degree below $2(p-1)$ and contribute nothing at $e$, while $AB$ differs from $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ only below degree $2(p-1)$, since replacing a linear form $f$ by $f-c$ alters $f^n$ only in degrees $<n$. Hence the coefficient of $X^e$ in $F$ is the given nonzero one, and $\deg F=2(p-1)=\sum_i e_i$. The Combinatorial Nullstellensatz produces $x$ with $x_i \in S_i$ and $F(x) \ne 0$; both factors are then nonzero, and $1-y^{p-1} \ne 0$ forces $y=0$ by Fermat's little theorem, giving $L_1(x)=t_1$, $L_2(x)=t_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Degree budget equals the conjectured bound]\label{thm:budget}
Let $k \ge 2$ and each $S_i$ be nonempty. An admissible exponent vector exists if and only if $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The available total exponent is $\sum_i(|S_i|-1)=k(p-1)-D(S)$, so a vector with $e_i \le |S_i|-1$ and $\sum_i e_i=2(p-1)$ exists iff $k(p-1)-D(S) \ge 2(p-1)$; sufficiency is realised by greedily filling the caps.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Structure of the conjecture]\label{thm:structure}
Under $D(S) \le (k-2)(p-1)$ with all $S_i$ nonempty, an admissible exponent vector always exists, and any admissible vector with nonzero coefficient in $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ proves spanning. Hence \eqref{eq:conj} can fail only through the simultaneous vanishing of \emph{all} admissible coefficients.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
In the harmonic family the caps are $(p-2,p-2,1,1,0,\dots,0)$, summing to exactly $2(p-1)$: there is precisely one admissible exponent vector, and its coefficient vanishes. The counterexample is thus not a violation of the polynomial method but a witness that the method's hypothesis is strictly stronger than the degree count --- the conjecture was the degree count mistaken for the hypothesis.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Reach computation by iterated sumset]
Start from $\{(0,0)\}$ and repeatedly replace the accumulator $R$ by $\{r+sv_i : r \in R,\ s \in S_i\}$. Since $|R| \le p^2$ throughout, the cost is $O\bigl(p^2\sum_i|S_i|\bigr)=O(kp^3)$, against $O\bigl(\prod_i|S_i|\bigr)$ for naive enumeration.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Spanning certificate]
Sort the deficiencies and test $d_{(1)}+d_{(2)}+d_{(3)}<p$; if it holds, output the witness triple. By Theorem~\ref{thm:triple} this is a proof of spanning, obtained in $O(k\log k)$ time with no computation in the plane.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Explicit representation along a triple]
Given a target $t$ and a certified triple, compute $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ by Cramer's rule and scan $c \in \FF_p$ until $c \in S_l$, $\alpha-\gamma c \in S_i$ and $\beta-\delta c \in S_j$. Theorem~\ref{thm:three} guarantees success within $d_i+d_j+d_l+1 \le p$ trials, so the cost is $O(p)$ field operations.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Admissible-coefficient search]
Expand $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ sparsely over $\FF_p$ and inspect all admissible coefficients. A nonzero one certifies spanning even when no triple criterion applies. The expansion has at most $\binom{k+2p-3}{2p-2}$ monomials.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Computational evidence}

Exhaustive and targeted computation supports and sharpens the theory. Over all pairwise independent triples and all step-sets containing $0$: at $p=3$ all $88$ configurations with $D<p$ span, and at $p=5$ all $15\,880$ do, while non-spanning configurations appear at $D=p$ exactly ($80$ and $14\,400$ respectively), so $D<p$ is precisely the right hypothesis. For $(p,k) \in \{(3,4),(5,4),(5,6),(7,5),(7,8),(11,6)\}$ the harmonic family has $D=(k-2)(p-1)$ and misses exactly the single point $(1,2)$, with minimum triple deficiency exactly $p$; and the image of its reach in each of the $k$ quotient lines has size exactly $p$, as Theorem~\ref{thm:quot} requires. At $p=5$, $k=4$, all $3\,797$ configurations with $S_1=\FF_5$ and $D \le 8$ span, in accordance with Theorem~\ref{thm:full}. Finally, for the harmonic counterexamples the unique admissible exponent vector has coefficient $0$, whereas a nearby spanning configuration at $p=5$, $k=4$ with $D=7$ has three nonzero admissible coefficients.

\section{Discussion}

The failure of \eqref{eq:conj} is a failure of \emph{aggregation}. Total deficiency is a single scalar, while spanning is a projective-geometric property, and the harmonic quadruple is precisely a configuration in which a large budget is spent so as to create an obstruction rather than diffuse slack. Two features make this vivid. First, the correct criterion is \emph{local}: three directions with joint deficiency below $p$ suffice, however impoverished the remaining $k-3$ directions are. Second, both natural derivations of $(k-2)(p-1)$ are correct as far as they go --- the degree count is exact (Theorem~\ref{thm:budget}) and the quotient count is exact (Theorem~\ref{thm:quot}); each simply proves a weaker conclusion than \eqref{eq:conj} claims. It is a good example of a conjecture that is not a wild guess but the conflation of a necessary condition with a sufficient one.

\section{Future directions}

\textbf{Profile dichotomy for spanning.} Fix $p$ and $k \ge 3$. Conjecturally, a deficiency profile $d_1 \le \cdots \le d_k$ admits some pairwise independent non-spanning configuration if and only if $d_1+d_2+d_3 \ge p$ \emph{and} the profile avoids an explicitly describable list of exceptions. The condition is exactly the failure of Theorem~\ref{thm:triple}, hence necessary; enumeration shows it is not sufficient. Every exception observed so far --- $(0,2,3,3)$, $(1,2,2,2)$, $(2,2,2,2)$ at $p=5$ and $(1,3,3,4)$ at $p=7$ --- is a profile in which no four indices can be arranged into a harmonic cross-ratio pattern with the available set sizes: the obstruction is projective, not merely numerical.

\textbf{Cross-ratio invariants.} The harmonic quadruple is characterised by cross-ratio $-1$. Is a non-spanning configuration at the extremal deficiency necessarily supported on a quadruple in harmonic position, up to projective equivalence?

\textbf{Higher dimensions.} The pencil argument suggests, for $\FF_p^n$ with directions in general position, the criterion ``some $(n+1)$-subset has deficiency sum $<p$''. The covering step uses one-dimensionality of the fibre essentially, so a new idea is needed.

\textbf{Non-prime moduli.} Over $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ Cauchy--Davenport is replaced by Kneser's stabiliser-corrected bound; the natural analogue of Theorem~\ref{thm:triple} should read ``the reach is everything unless a coset of a proper subgroup obstructs''.

\textbf{Quantitative refinement of ``no missing line''.} Under $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$, is the missed set always of size at most $1$? Computation supports this for small $p$ and $k$; a proof would show \eqref{eq:conj} fails only in the mildest conceivable way.

\textbf{Effective inverse theory.} Given a non-spanning configuration, can the missed point be read off from the direction family and the set sizes in $O(k)$ time? For the harmonic family the answer is $(1,2)$ up to projective normalisation.

\section{Summary of results}

Let $p$ be prime, $v_1,\dots,v_k$ pairwise independent in $\FF_p^2$, $S_i \ni 0$, $d_i=p-|S_i|$, $D=\sum_i d_i$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $k=3$: $d_1+d_2+d_3<p$ implies spanning, sharply.
\item For any $k \ge 3$: some triple with $d_i+d_j+d_l<p$ implies spanning; in particular $D \le p-1$ suffices.
\item For every prime $p \ge 3$ and every $k$ with $4 \le k \le p+1$ there is a configuration with $D=(k-2)(p-1)$ that does not span.
\item In that family every triple has deficiency sum $\ge p$ with equality attained, so (2) is optimal.
\item If some $S_{i_0}=\FF_p$, then $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ does imply spanning.
\item $D \le (k-2)(p-1)$ implies the reach meets every line parallel to every $v_i$.
\item $(k-2)(p-1)$ is exactly the degree budget making an admissible monomial of $L_1^{p-1}L_2^{p-1}$ available; the conjecture can fail only by simultaneous vanishing of all admissible coefficients, as it does in the harmonic family.
\end{enumerate}

The *deficiency* of S_i is d_i = p - |S_i|, and the total deficiency is
D = d_1 + ... + d_k.

This script demonstrates, by exhaustive computation over small primes:

  1. Three-line theorem:  k = 3 and d_1 + d_2 + d_3 < p  ==>  Reach = F_p^2,

  2. Triple criterion:  for arbitrary k, if SOME three distinct indices have

  3. Refutation of the (k-2)(p-1) conjecture: the harmonic family
     (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (-1,1) with S_1 = S_2 = F_p \ {1}, S_3 = S_4 = {0,1}
     (padded by {0}) has total deficiency exactly (k-2)(p-1) and misses (1,2).
  4. Sharpness of the triple criterion in that same family: every triple of
     distinct indices has deficiency sum >= p, with p attained.
  5. What the conjectured bound does buy: surjectivity onto every quotient
     line, i.e. the reach meets every line parallel to each v_i.
  6. The "one full set" theorem: if some S_i = F_p, the conjectured bound
     (k-2)(p-1) is valid after all (iterated Cauchy-Davenport).
  7. The polynomial-method picture: all admissible coefficients of
     L_1^{p-1} L_2^{p-1} vanish exactly in the counterexample configurations.

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic arithmetic in F_p^2
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def det(a: Vec, b: Vec, p: int) -> int:
    """Determinant a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 in F_p."""
    return (a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0]) % p


def pairwise_independent(v: Sequence[Vec], p: int) -> bool:
    """True iff det(v_i, v_j) != 0 for all i != j."""
    return all(det(v[i], v[j], p) != 0 for i, j in combinations(range(len(v)), 2))


def reach(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> Set[Vec]:
    """All points s_1 v_1 + ... + s_k v_k with s_i in S_i (breadth-first sumset)."""
    acc: Set[Vec] = {(0, 0)}
    for vec, Si in zip(v, S):
        acc = {((x + s * vec[0]) % p, (y + s * vec[1]) % p) for (x, y) in acc for s in Si}
    return acc


def deficiencies(S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """d_i = p - |S_i|."""
    return [p - len(set(Si)) for Si in S]


def spans(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> bool:
    return len(reach(v, S, p)) == p * p


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The three-line theorem and its sharpness
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def subsets_containing_zero(p: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All subsets of F_p containing 0, as sorted tuples."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    rest = list(range(1, p))
    for mask in range(1 << (p - 1)):
        out.append(tuple([0] + [rest[i] for i in range(p - 1) if mask >> i & 1]))
    return out


def check_three_line_theorem(p: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Exhaustively verify: three pairwise independent directions and sets with
    total deficiency < p always span.  Returns (#hypothesis-satisfying triples,
    #non-spanning configurations at deficiency exactly p)."""
    dirs = [(1, m) for m in range(p)] + [(0, 1)]  # the p+1 projective directions
    subs = subsets_containing_zero(p)
    verified = 0
    sharp_witnesses = 0
    for v in combinations(dirs, 3):
        if not pairwise_independent(v, p):
            continue
        for S in product(subs, repeat=3):
            D = sum(deficiencies(S, p))
            if D < p:
                assert spans(v, S, p), f"counterexample to the three-line theorem: {v}, {S}"
                verified += 1
            elif D == p and not spans(v, S, p):
                sharp_witnesses += 1
    return verified, sharp_witnesses


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2/3/4. The harmonic counterexample family
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def harmonic_family(p: int, k: int) -> Tuple[List[Vec], List[List[int]]]:
    """The counterexample family: directions (1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(-1,1) followed by
    (1, j-2) for j >= 4, and sets F_p\\{1}, F_p\\{1}, {0,1}, {0,1}, {0}, ..., {0}.
    Requires 4 <= k <= p+1 and p >= 3."""
    assert p >= 3 and 4 <= k <= p + 1
    v: List[Vec] = [(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (p - 1, 1)]
    v += [(1, (j - 2) % p) for j in range(4, k)]
    S: List[List[int]] = [
        [x for x in range(p) if x != 1],
        [x for x in range(p) if x != 1],
        [0, 1],
        [0, 1],
    ]
    S += [[0] for _ in range(4, k)]
    return v, S


def check_harmonic_counterexample(p: int, k: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Verify: pairwise independence, deficiency exactly (k-2)(p-1), (1,2) missing,
    every triple deficiency sum >= p with equality attained."""
    v, S = harmonic_family(p, k)
    d = deficiencies(S, p)
    R = reach(v, S, p)
    triples = [d[i] + d[j] + d[l] for i, j, l in combinations(range(k), 3)]
    return {
        "p": p,
        "k": k,
        "pairwise_independent": pairwise_independent(v, p),
        "total_deficiency": sum(d),
        "conjectured_bound": (k - 2) * (p - 1),
        "misses_(1,2)": (1, 2 % p) not in R,
        "missing_points": sorted(set(product(range(p), repeat=2)) - R),
        "min_triple_deficiency": min(triples),
        "all_triples_at_least_p": min(triples) >= p,
    }


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Surjectivity onto quotient lines
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def quotient_image(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int, i0: int) -> Set[int]:
    """The image of the reach under r |-> det(r, v_{i0}); i.e. which lines parallel
    to v_{i0} the reach meets."""
    return {det(r, v[i0], p) for r in reach(v, S, p)}


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The "one full set" theorem
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_one_full_set(p: int, k: int, trials: Iterable[Sequence[Tuple[int, ...]]]) -> int:
    """For configurations in which S_0 = F_p and the total deficiency is at most
    (k-2)(p-1), verify that the reach is everything.  Returns the number checked."""
    dirs = [(1, m) for m in range(p)] + [(0, 1)]
    v = dirs[:k]
    assert pairwise_independent(v, p)
    checked = 0
    for tail in trials:
        S = [tuple(range(p))] + list(tail)
        if len(S) != k:
            continue
        if sum(deficiencies(S, p)) <= (k - 2) * (p - 1):
            assert spans(v, S, p), f"unexpected failure: {S}"
            checked += 1
    return checked


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The polynomial-method picture
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def multiply(f: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int], g: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int],
             p: int) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]:
    """Multiply two sparse multivariate polynomials over F_p (exponent tuples)."""
    h: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {}
    for e1, c1 in f.items():
        for e2, c2 in g.items():
            e = tuple(a + b for a, b in zip(e1, e2))
            h[e] = (h.get(e, 0) + c1 * c2) % p
    return {e: c for e, c in h.items() if c % p}


def lin_form(w: Sequence[int], k: int, p: int) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]:
    """The linear form sum_i w_i X_i as a sparse polynomial."""
    f: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {}
    for i in range(k):
        if w[i] % p:
            e = tuple(1 if j == i else 0 for j in range(k))
            f[e] = w[i] % p
    return f


def power(f: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int], n: int, k: int,
          p: int) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]:
    res: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {tuple(0 for _ in range(k)): 1}
    for _ in range(n):
        res = multiply(res, f, p)
    return res


def admissible_coefficients(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]],
                            p: int) -> List[Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], int]]:
    """All coefficients of L_1^{p-1} L_2^{p-1} at exponent vectors e with
    e_i < |S_i| and sum(e) = 2(p-1).  A single nonzero one certifies spanning."""
    k = len(v)
    L1 = lin_form([a for a, _ in v], k, p)
    L2 = lin_form([b for _, b in v], k, p)
    P = multiply(power(L1, p - 1, k, p), power(L2, p - 1, k, p), p)
    out = []
    caps = [len(set(Si)) - 1 for Si in S]
    for e in product(*[range(c + 1) for c in caps]):
        if sum(e) == 2 * (p - 1):
            out.append((e, P.get(e, 0) % p))
    return out

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic arithmetic in F_p^2
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def det(a: Vec, b: Vec, p: int) -> int:
    """Determinant a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 in F_p."""
    return (a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0]) % p


def pairwise_independent(v: Sequence[Vec], p: int) -> bool:
    """True iff det(v_i, v_j) != 0 for all i != j."""
    return all(det(v[i], v[j], p) != 0 for i, j in combinations(range(len(v)), 2))


def reach(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> Set[Vec]:
    """All points s_1 v_1 + ... + s_k v_k with s_i in S_i (breadth-first sumset)."""
    acc: Set[Vec] = {(0, 0)}
    for vec, Si in zip(v, S):
        acc = {((x + s * vec[0]) % p, (y + s * vec[1]) % p) for (x, y) in acc for s in Si}
    return acc


def deficiencies(S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> List[int]:
    """d_i = p - |S_i|."""
    return [p - len(set(Si)) for Si in S]


def spans(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> bool:
    return len(reach(v, S, p)) == p * p


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The three-line theorem and its sharpness
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def subsets_containing_zero(p: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All subsets of F_p containing 0, as sorted tuples."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    rest = list(range(1, p))
    for mask in range(1 << (p - 1)):
        out.append(tuple([0] + [rest[i] for i in range(p - 1) if mask >> i & 1]))
    return out


def check_three_line_theorem(p: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Exhaustively verify: three pairwise independent directions and sets with
    total deficiency < p always span.  Returns (#hypothesis-satisfying triples,
    #non-spanning configurations at deficiency exactly p)."""
    dirs = [(1, m) for m in range(p)] + [(0, 1)]  # the p+1 projective directions
    subs = subsets_containing_zero(p)
    verified = 0
    sharp_witnesses = 0
    for v in combinations(dirs, 3):
        if not pairwise_independent(v, p):
            continue
        for S in product(subs, repeat=3):
            D = sum(deficiencies(S, p))
            if D < p:
                assert spans(v, S, p), f"counterexample to the three-line theorem: {v}, {S}"
                verified += 1
            elif D == p and not spans(v, S, p):
                sharp_witnesses += 1
    return verified, sharp_witnesses


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2/3/4. The harmonic counterexample family
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def harmonic_family(p: int, k: int) -> Tuple[List[Vec], List[List[int]]]:
    """The counterexample family: directions (1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(-1,1) followed by
    (1, j-2) for j >= 4, and sets F_p\\{1}, F_p\\{1}, {0,1}, {0,1}, {0}, ..., {0}.
    Requires 4 <= k <= p+1 and p >= 3."""
    assert p >= 3 and 4 <= k <= p + 1
    v: List[Vec] = [(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (p - 1, 1)]
    v += [(1, (j - 2) % p) for j in range(4, k)]
    S: List[List[int]] = [
        [x for x in range(p) if x != 1],
        [x for x in range(p) if x != 1],
        [0, 1],
        [0, 1],
    ]
    S += [[0] for _ in range(4, k)]
    return v, S


def check_harmonic_counterexample(p: int, k: int) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Verify: pairwise independence, deficiency exactly (k-2)(p-1), (1,2) missing,
    every triple deficiency sum >= p with equality attained."""
    v, S = harmonic_family(p, k)
    d = deficiencies(S, p)
    R = reach(v, S, p)
    triples = [d[i] + d[j] + d[l] for i, j, l in combinations(range(k), 3)]
    return {
        "p": p,
        "k": k,
        "pairwise_independent": pairwise_independent(v, p),
        "total_deficiency": sum(d),
        "conjectured_bound": (k - 2) * (p - 1),
        "misses_(1,2)": (1, 2 % p) not in R,
        "missing_points": sorted(set(product(range(p), repeat=2)) - R),
        "min_triple_deficiency": min(triples),
        "all_triples_at_least_p": min(triples) >= p,
    }


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Surjectivity onto quotient lines
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def quotient_image(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int, i0: int) -> Set[int]:
    """The image of the reach under r |-> det(r, v_{i0}); i.e. which lines parallel
    to v_{i0} the reach meets."""
    return {det(r, v[i0], p) for r in reach(v, S, p)}


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The "one full set" theorem
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def check_one_full_set(p: int, k: int, trials: Iterable[Sequence[Tuple[int, ...]]]) -> int:
    """For configurations in which S_0 = F_p and the total deficiency is at most
    (k-2)(p-1), verify that the reach is everything.  Returns the number checked."""
    dirs = [(1, m) for m in range(p)] + [(0, 1)]
    v = dirs[:k]
    assert pairwise_independent(v, p)
    checked = 0
    for tail in trials:
        S = [tuple(range(p))] + list(tail)
        if len(S) != k:
            continue
        if sum(deficiencies(S, p)) <= (k - 2) * (p - 1):
            assert spans(v, S, p), f"unexpected failure: {S}"
            checked += 1
    return checked


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The polynomial-method picture
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def multiply(f: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int], g: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int],
             p: int) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]:
    """Multiply two sparse multivariate polynomials over F_p (exponent tuples)."""
    h: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {}
    for e1, c1 in f.items():
        for e2, c2 in g.items():
            e = tuple(a + b for a, b in zip(e1, e2))
            h[e] = (h.get(e, 0) + c1 * c2) % p
    return {e: c for e, c in h.items() if c % p}


def lin_form(w: Sequence[int], k: int, p: int) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]:
    """The linear form sum_i w_i X_i as a sparse polynomial."""
    f: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {}
    for i in range(k):
        if w[i] % p:
            e = tuple(1 if j == i else 0 for j in range(k))
            f[e] = w[i] % p
    return f


def power(f: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int], n: int, k: int,
          p: int) -> Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]:
    res: Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int] = {tuple(0 for _ in range(k)): 1}
    for _ in range(n):
        res = multiply(res, f, p)
    return res


def admissible_coefficients(v: Sequence[Vec], S: Sequence[Sequence[int]],
                            p: int) -> List[Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], int]]:
    """All coefficients of L_1^{p-1} L_2^{p-1} at exponent vectors e with
    e_i < |S_i| and sum(e) = 2(p-1).  A single nonzero one certifies spanning."""
    k = len(v)
    L1 = lin_form([a for a, _ in v], k, p)
    L2 = lin_form([b for _, b in v], k, p)
    P = multiply(power(L1, p - 1, k, p), power(L2, p - 1, k, p), p)
    out = []
    caps = [len(set(Si)) - 1 for Si in S]
    for e in product(*[range(c + 1) for c in caps]):
        if sum(e) == 2 * (p - 1):
            out.append((e, P.get(e, 0) % p))
    return out

def deficiencies(p: int, step_sets: Sequence[Iterable[int]]) -> List[int]:
    """d_i = p - |S_i|."""

def triple_certificate(p: int, step_sets: Sequence[Iterable[int]]
                       ) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Return a triple of indices (i, j, l) with d_i + d_j + d_l < p, or None.

    By the triple criterion, such a triple proves that the reach is all of F_p^2,
    whatever the other directions do — provided the directions are pairwise
    non-parallel and every step-set contains 0.  Since the three smallest
    deficiencies minimise the sum, it suffices to sort: O(k log k).
    """
    d = deficiencies(p, step_sets)
    order = sorted(range(len(d)), key=lambda i: d[i])
    if len(order) < 3:
        return None
    i, j, l = order[0], order[1], order[2]
    return (i, j, l) if d[i] + d[j] + d[l] < p else None


def pairwise_independent(p: int, directions: Sequence[Vec]) -> bool:
    """det(v_i, v_j) != 0 for all i != j."""
    k = len(directions)
    for i in range(k):
        for j in range(i + 1, k):
            a, b = directions[i], directions[j]
            if (a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0]) % p == 0:
                return False
    return True

    t = triple_certificate(p, step_sets)
    d = deficiencies(p, step_sets)
    if t is None:

                f"(the configuration may or may not span)")

    return (f"SPANS: triple ({i},{j},{l}) has deficiencies "
            f"{d[i]}+{d[j]}+{d[l]} = {d[i]+d[j]+d[l]} < p = {p}")

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]


def inv_mod(a: int, p: int) -> int:
    """Inverse in F_p (p prime, a not divisible by p)."""
    return pow(a % p, p - 2, p)


def det(a: Vec, b: Vec, p: int) -> int:
    return (a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0]) % p


def decode_along_triple(p: int, v1: Vec, v2: Vec, v3: Vec,
                        S1: Iterable[int], S2: Iterable[int], S3: Iterable[int],
                        target: Vec) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int, int]]:
    """Find (s_1, s_2, s_3) in S_1 x S_2 x S_3 with s_1 v_1 + s_2 v_2 + s_3 v_3 = target.

    Method: (v_1, v_2) is a basis, so writing target = alpha v_1 + beta v_2 and
    v_3 = gamma v_1 + delta v_2 (Cramer's rule), every representation is
    (alpha - gamma c, beta - delta c, c) for a single scalar c.  Scanning c over
    F_p costs O(p) field operations, and the three-line theorem guarantees success
    within d_1 + d_2 + d_3 + 1 <= p trials whenever d_1 + d_2 + d_3 < p.
    """
    A1, A2, A3 = set(x % p for x in S1), set(x % p for x in S2), set(x % p for x in S3)
    D = det(v1, v2, p)
    if D == 0:
        raise ValueError("v1 and v2 are parallel")
    Dinv = inv_mod(D, p)
    alpha = det(target, v2, p) * Dinv % p
    beta = det(v1, target, p) * Dinv % p
    gamma = det(v3, v2, p) * Dinv % p
    delta = det(v1, v3, p) * Dinv % p
    for c in range(p):
        if c not in A3:
            continue
        s1 = (alpha - gamma * c) % p
        s2 = (beta - delta * c) % p
        if s1 in A1 and s2 in A2:
            return (s1, s2, c)
    return None


def decode_full_configuration(p: int, directions: Sequence[Vec],
                              step_sets: Sequence[List[int]],
                              triple: Tuple[int, int, int],
                              target: Vec) -> Optional[Dict[int, int]]:
    """Decode along the certified triple and pad the other coefficients with 0."""
    i, j, l = triple
    sol = decode_along_triple(p, directions[i], directions[j], directions[l],
                              step_sets[i], step_sets[j], step_sets[l], target)
    if sol is None:
        return None
    coeffs = {m: 0 for m in range(len(directions))}
    coeffs[i], coeffs[j], coeffs[l] = sol
    return coeffs

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Vec = Tuple[int, int]
Poly = Dict[Tuple[int, ...], int]


def poly_mul(f: Poly, g: Poly, p: int) -> Poly:
    """Multiply sparse multivariate polynomials over F_p."""
    h: Poly = {}
    for e1, c1 in f.items():
        for e2, c2 in g.items():
            e = tuple(a + b for a, b in zip(e1, e2))
            h[e] = (h.get(e, 0) + c1 * c2) % p
    return {e: c for e, c in h.items() if c}


def linear_form(weights: Sequence[int], p: int) -> Poly:
    """sum_i w_i X_i as a sparse polynomial in k variables."""
    k = len(weights)
    f: Poly = {}
    for i, w in enumerate(weights):
        if w % p:
            f[tuple(1 if j == i else 0 for j in range(k))] = w % p
    return f


def poly_pow(f: Poly, n: int, k: int, p: int) -> Poly:
    """Repeated squaring for f^n over F_p."""
    result: Poly = {tuple(0 for _ in range(k)): 1}
    base = dict(f)
    while n:
        if n & 1:
            result = poly_mul(result, base, p)
        base = poly_mul(base, base, p)
        n >>= 1
    return result


def admissible_certificate(p: int, directions: Sequence[Vec],
                           step_sets: Sequence[Iterable[int]]
                           ) -> Optional[Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], int]]:
    """Search for an exponent vector e with e_i < |S_i| and sum(e) = 2(p-1) whose
    coefficient in L_1^{p-1} L_2^{p-1} is nonzero.

    Such an e certifies that the reach is all of F_p^2, by the Combinatorial
    Nullstellensatz.  An admissible e exists at all precisely when the total
    deficiency is at most (k-2)(p-1); the certificate additionally requires the
    coefficient to survive.  The expansion has at most C(k + 2p - 3, 2p - 2)
    monomials, so the procedure is exponential in p but practical for small
    parameters.
    """
    k = len(directions)
    L1 = linear_form([v[0] for v in directions], p)
    L2 = linear_form([v[1] for v in directions], p)
    P = poly_mul(poly_pow(L1, p - 1, k, p), poly_pow(L2, p - 1, k, p), p)
    caps = [len(set(S)) - 1 for S in step_sets]
    for e in product(*[range(c + 1) for c in caps]):
        if sum(e) == 2 * (p - 1):
            c = P.get(e, 0) % p
            if c:
                return (e, c)
    return None


def report(p: int, directions: Sequence[Vec], step_sets: Sequence[List[int]]) -> str:
    k = len(directions)
    d = [p - len(set(S)) for S in step_sets]
    budget_ok = sum(d) <= (k - 2) * (p - 1)
    cert = admissible_certificate(p, directions, step_sets)
    head = (f"p={p}, k={k}, D={sum(d)}, budget (k-2)(p-1)={(k-2)*(p-1)}: "
            f"admissible exponents {'exist' if budget_ok else 'do NOT exist'}")
    if cert is None:
        return head + "; every admissible coefficient vanishes — criterion silent"
    return head + f"; certificate e={cert[0]} with coefficient {cert[1]} — SPANS"

<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Reach Laboratory</h1>
  <p class="lede">

    <span class="mono">F_p²</span>, and switch individual step-lengths on and off. The panel on the

          <option value="5" selected>5</option>

        <button class="preset" data-preset="triple">rich triple</button>

<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";

  var pSel = document.getElementById("pSel");
  var kSel = document.getElementById("kSel");
  var dirBody = document.getElementById("dirBody");
  var canvas = document.getElementById("board");
  var ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  var verdict = document.getElementById("verdict");
  var reprBox = document.getElementById("repr");

  var state = { p: 5, k: 4, slopes: [], sets: [], selected: null };

  // ---- projective directions: slope m gives (1,m); slope "inf" gives (0,1) ----
  function slopeOptions(p) {
    var out = [];
    for (var m = 0; m < p; m++) out.push(String(m));
    out.push("inf");
    return out;
  }
  function vecOf(slope, p) {
    return slope === "inf" ? [0, 1] : [1, ((parseInt(slope, 10) % p) + p) % p];
  }
  function det(a, b, p) { return (((a[0] * b[1] - a[1] * b[0]) % p) + p) % p; }

  function defaultSlopes(p, k) {
    var pref = ["0", "inf", "1", String(p - 1), "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"];
    var out = [], i;
    for (i = 0; i < pref.length && out.length < k; i++) {
      var s = pref[i];
      if (s === "inf" || (parseInt(s, 10) < p)) {
        if (out.indexOf(s) === -1) out.push(s);
      }
    }
    var all = slopeOptions(p);
    for (i = 0; out.length < k && i < all.length; i++) {
      if (out.indexOf(all[i]) === -1) out.push(all[i]);
    }
    return out.slice(0, k);
  }

  function fullSet(p) { var s = []; for (var i = 0; i < p; i++) s.push(true); return s; }

  // ---- presets -------------------------------------------------------------
  function applyPreset(name) {
    var p = state.p, k = state.k, i, j;
    if (name === "harmonic") {
      state.slopes = defaultSlopes(p, k);            // 0, inf, 1, -1, then others
      state.sets = [];
      for (i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        var S = [];
        for (j = 0; j < p; j++) S.push(false);
        S[0] = true;
        if (i === 0 || i === 1) { for (j = 0; j < p; j++) S[j] = (j !== 1); }
        else if (i === 2 || i === 3) { S[1 % p] = true; }
        state.sets.push(S);
      }
    } else if (name === "triple") {
      state.slopes = defaultSlopes(p, k);
      state.sets = [];
      for (i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        var T = [];
        for (j = 0; j < p; j++) T.push(i < 3 ? true : false);
        T[0] = true;
        if (i < 3 && p > 3) T[p - 1] = false;         // small deficiency each
        state.sets.push(T);
      }
    } else if (name === "full") {
      state.slopes = defaultSlopes(p, k);
      state.sets = [];
      var budget = (k - 2) * (p - 1);
      var q = Math.floor(budget / Math.max(1, k - 1));   // deficiency of each other set
      for (i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        var U = [];
        for (j = 0; j < p; j++) U.push(i === 0 ? true : (j < p - q));
        U[0] = true;
        state.sets.push(U);
      }
    } else {
      state.slopes = defaultSlopes(p, k);
      state.sets = [];
      for (i = 0; i < k; i++) state.sets.push(fullSet(p));
    }
    state.selected = null;
    render();
  }

  // ---- reach with backpointers --------------------------------------------
  function computeLayers() {
    var p = state.p, k = state.k, N = p * p, i, idx, s;
    var layers = [];
    var cur = new Array(N).fill(null);
    cur[0] = { prev: -1, s: 0 };
    layers.push(cur);
    for (i = 0; i < k; i++) {
      var v = vecOf(state.slopes[i], p);
      var nxt = new Array(N).fill(null);
      for (idx = 0; idx < N; idx++) {
        if (!cur[idx]) continue;
        var x = idx % p, y = (idx - x) / p;
        for (s = 0; s < p; s++) {
          if (!state.sets[i][s]) continue;
          var nx = (x + s * v[0]) % p, ny = (y + s * v[1]) % p;
          var nidx = ny * p + nx;
          if (!nxt[nidx]) nxt[nidx] = { prev: idx, s: s };
        }
      }
      cur = nxt;
      layers.push(cur);
    }
    return layers;
  }

  function representation(layers, idx) {
    var k = state.k, coeffs = new Array(k).fill(0), cur = idx, i;
    if (!layers[k][cur]) return null;
    for (i = k; i >= 1; i--) {
      var rec = layers[i][cur];
      coeffs[i - 1] = rec.s;
      cur = rec.prev;
    }
    return coeffs;
  }

  // ---- rendering -----------------------------------------------------------
  function buildTable() {
    var p = state.p, k = state.k, html = "", i, j;
    var opts = slopeOptions(p);
    for (i = 0; i < k; i++) {
      var v = vecOf(state.slopes[i], p);
      html += "<tr><td class='mono'>" + i + "</td><td><select data-dir='" + i + "'>";
      for (j = 0; j < opts.length; j++) {
        var lab = opts[j] === "inf" ? "(0,1)" : "(1," + opts[j] + ")";
        html += "<option value='" + opts[j] + "'" +
                (opts[j] === state.slopes[i] ? " selected" : "") + ">" + lab + "</option>";
      }
      html += "</select></td><td><div class='chips'>";
      for (j = 0; j < p; j++) {
        var on = state.sets[i][j];
        html += "<span class='chip" + (on ? " on" : "") + (j === 0 ? " locked" : "") +
                "' data-set='" + i + "' data-val='" + j + "'>" + j + "</span>";
      }
      html += "</div></td><td class='mono'>" + (p - state.sets[i].filter(Boolean).length) +
              "</td></tr>";
      void v;
    }
    dirBody.innerHTML = html;

    Array.prototype.forEach.call(dirBody.querySelectorAll("select"), function (sel) {
      sel.addEventListener("change", function () {
        state.slopes[parseInt(sel.getAttribute("data-dir"), 10)] = sel.value;
        state.selected = null;
        render();
      });
    });
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(dirBody.querySelectorAll(".chip"), function (chip) {
      chip.addEventListener("click", function () {
        var i = parseInt(chip.getAttribute("data-set"), 10);
        var val = parseInt(chip.getAttribute("data-val"), 10);
        if (val === 0) return;                     // 0 is always available
        state.sets[i][val] = !state.sets[i][val];
        state.selected = null;
        render();
      });
    });
  }

  function drawBoard(layers) {
    var p = state.p, k = state.k, N = p * p;
    var W = canvas.width, pad = 26, cell = (W - 2 * pad) / (p - 1 || 1);
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#eef2f8"; ctx.lineWidth = 1;
    for (var g = 0; g < p; g++) {
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(pad + g * cell, pad); ctx.lineTo(pad + g * cell, W - pad); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(pad, pad + g * cell); ctx.lineTo(W - pad, pad + g * cell); ctx.stroke();
    }
    var r = Math.max(4, Math.min(13, 120 / p));
    for (var idx = 0; idx < N; idx++) {
      var x = idx % p, y = (idx - x) / p;
      var cx = pad + x * cell, cy = W - pad - y * cell;
      var reached = !!layers[k][idx];
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx, cy, r, 0, 2 * Math.PI);
      ctx.fillStyle = reached ? "#2a6ebb" : "#d1495b";
      ctx.globalAlpha = reached ? 0.9 : 1;
      ctx.fill(); ctx.globalAlpha = 1;
      if (state.selected === idx) {
        ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx, cy, r + 4, 0, 2 * Math.PI);
        ctx.strokeStyle = "#f0a202"; ctx.lineWidth = 3; ctx.stroke();
      }
    }
  }

  function render() {
    var p = state.p, k = state.k, i, j, l;
    buildTable();
    // pairwise independence check
    var indep = true;
    for (i = 0; i < k; i++) for (j = i + 1; j < k; j++) {
      if (det(vecOf(state.slopes[i], p), vecOf(state.slopes[j], p), p) === 0) indep = false;
    }
    var d = state.sets.map(function (S) { return p - S.filter(Boolean).length; });
    var D = d.reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0);
    var budget = (k - 2) * (p - 1);
    var sorted = d.slice().sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; });
    var triple = sorted[0] + sorted[1] + sorted[2];

    var layers = computeLayers();
    var reached = layers[k].filter(Boolean).length;

    document.getElementById("statD").textContent = D;
    document.getElementById("statBudget").textContent = budget;
    document.getElementById("statTriple").textContent = triple + (triple < p ? " < p" : " ≥ p");
    document.getElementById("statReach").textContent = reached + " / " + (p * p);

    var cls, msg;
    if (!indep) {
      cls = "warn";
      msg = "Two directions coincide — the family is not pairwise non-parallel, so none of the " +
            "criteria apply. Change a direction.";
    } else if (triple < p) {
      cls = "good";
      msg = "The triple criterion applies: the three smallest deficiencies sum to " + triple +
            " < p = " + p + ", so the reach must be — and is — the whole plane.";
    } else if (reached === p * p) {
      cls = "good";
      msg = "The reach is everything, but no triple certifies it (smallest triple sum " + triple +
            " ≥ p). Configurations like this are why the triple criterion is sufficient, not necessary.";
    } else {
      cls = "bad";
      msg = "The reach misses " + (p * p - reached) + " point" + (p * p - reached === 1 ? "" : "s") +
            ". Total deficiency D = " + D + (D <= budget ?
            " is within the conjectured budget " + budget + " — so the conjectured threshold is refuted here."
            : " exceeds the conjectured budget " + budget + ".") +
            " Note that no whole line is missed.";
    }
    verdict.className = "verdict " + cls;
    verdict.textContent = msg;

    drawBoard(layers);

    if (state.selected === null) {
      reprBox.textContent = "Click a point of the grid to decode it.";
    } else {
      var idx = state.selected, x = idx % p, y = (idx - x) / p;
      var coeffs = representation(layers, idx);
      if (!coeffs) {
        reprBox.innerHTML = "<b>(" + x + "," + y + ")</b> is <b style='color:#d1495b'>not reachable</b>: " +
          "every choice of step-lengths is blocked by a forbidden value.";
      } else {
        var parts = [];
        for (l = 0; l < k; l++) {
          var v = vecOf(state.slopes[l], p);
          parts.push(coeffs[l] + "·(" + v[0] + "," + v[1] + ")");
        }
        reprBox.innerHTML = "<b>(" + x + "," + y + ")</b> = <span class='mono'>" +
          parts.join(" + ") + "</span>";
      }
    }
  }

  canvas.addEventListener("click", function (ev) {
    var p = state.p, W = canvas.width, pad = 26, cell = (W - 2 * pad) / (p - 1 || 1);
    var rect = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
    var mx = (ev.clientX - rect.left) * canvas.width / rect.width;
    var my = (ev.clientY - rect.top) * canvas.height / rect.height;
    var x = Math.round((mx - pad) / cell), y = Math.round((W - pad - my) / cell);
    if (x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= p || y >= p) return;
    state.selected = y * p + x;
    render();
  });

  pSel.addEventListener("change", function () {
    state.p = parseInt(pSel.value, 10);
    var maxK = state.p + 1;
    if (state.k > maxK) { state.k = maxK; kSel.value = String(maxK); }
    applyPreset("harmonic");
  });
  kSel.addEventListener("change", function () {
    var want = parseInt(kSel.value, 10);
    state.k = Math.min(want, state.p + 1);
    kSel.value = String(state.k);
    applyPreset("harmonic");
  });
  Array.prototype.forEach.call(document.querySelectorAll("button.preset"), function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { applyPreset(b.getAttribute("data-preset")); });
  });

  applyPreset("harmonic");
})();
</script>
</body>

  "interactive_layout": "# Three Lines Are Enough — A Guided Tour

Welcome. By the end of this page you will know exactly when a handful of restricted
"step-sets" along fixed directions can reach every point of a finite plane — and why a
very natural-looking rule for it is false.

---

## 1. The game

Fix a prime $p$ and work in the plane $\mathbb{F}_p^2$: pairs $(x,y)$ of integers modulo
$p$, so exactly $p^2$ points. You are given $k$ **directions** $v_1,\dots,v_k$, no two of
them parallel, and along each direction a set $S_i \subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ of permitted
**step-lengths**, always containing $0$. Starting at the origin you take one step along
each direction and land on
$$s_1v_1 + s_2v_2 + \cdots + s_kv_k, \qquad s_i \in S_i .$$
The set of all landing points is the **reach** $\mathcal{R}$.

The natural measure of how crippled a step-set is, is its **deficiency**
$d_i = p - |S_i|$: the number of step-lengths you are *not* allowed to use. The **total
deficiency** is $D = d_1 + \cdots + d_k$.

> **The question.** How much deficiency can you afford before the reach stops being the
> whole plane?

<details>
<summary>Why insist that $0 \in S_i$?</summary>

Two reasons. First, it is only a normalisation: translating each step-set translates the
reach by a fixed vector, so nothing is lost. Second, and crucially, it means you may
always <em>skip</em> a direction. That is what lets a good sub-configuration carry the
whole family — the single most useful structural fact in this subject. Background on this
style of problem: <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumset">sumsets</a> and
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Davenport_theorem">the
Cauchy–Davenport theorem</a>.
</details>
